title: What a financial sandbox actually does
label: 18 November 2026 · Financial sandbox experiences
summary: Four businesses described very different experiences of regulatory sandboxes: programmes that let firms test products, sometimes with limited permission to carry out regulated activities. Two used them as a route towards authorisation, one is helping shape rules for a new kind of financial infrastructure, and another is developing software to help firms comply with existing rules. The witnesses generally valued the chance to test and speak to regulators, but disagreed about how well sandboxes connect firms to authorisation, other businesses and useful regulatory expertise. They urged the committee to be clearer about what each programme is meant to achieve.

glossary.definition: The Financial Conduct Authority, which regulates financial firms and markets in the UK.
A system that lets people securely share their bank-account information with authorised services.
FCA rules requiring financial firms to consider whether their products and services deliver good outcomes for customers.
Formal permission from a regulator for a firm to carry out specified financial activities.
Money held electronically by a firm for customers to use in payments.
A Bank of England and FCA programme for testing how financial investments can be issued and handled using new technology.
A digital token designed to maintain a stable value against an asset such as a currency.
Artificially created information used to test a system without relying on real customers' records.

chapters.title: Why they joined
chapters.takeaway: The firms entered sandboxes for different reasons, from testing compliance software to obtaining permission to offer financial services.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Why did you enter a sandbox, and has it met your expectations?

evidence.quote: Why did you go into the sandbox and how is it living up to your expectations?

turns.speaker: Lyubomira Dimitrova
turns.text: Relace makes software to help firms follow financial rules. We're in a current FCA sandbox because we want to understand consumer duty—rules that affect many parts of a firm—and why firms struggle to put it into practice. The experience has been positive, though some parts have been challenging.

evidence.quote: Relace is a regulatory technology platform and product. We are currently part of the FCA supercharged sandbox cohort 2, which runs from July until the end of the year, so we are a current participant.

The product that we have developed is for consumer duty, which is a very recent regime. It is only three years old and a lot of the firms out there are struggling to figure out how to do it well, because it touches all parts of a company.
The experience has been positive. There are areas that have been challenging as well.

turns.speaker: Kevin Sefton
turns.text: Untied helps people use open banking information to prepare tax returns. When we joined in 2019, we needed FCA permission to use that information. We thought the sandbox would get us there faster than applying directly. For us, the immediate need wasn't to prove something radically new; it was to become regulated.

evidence.quote: Untied, which is a personal tax software product that helps people categorise transactions from open banking and other sources. They use Untied to file their self-assessment and now Making Tax Digital. We were in the fifth cohort of the FCA sandbox in 2019
At the time, you needed direct regulation from the FCA in order to do that. We had a choice of whether we went for the full regulation or for the sandbox.
It was not about innovation. It was the simple need to be regulated, and we thought and hoped that the sandbox would be the quickest way to do it.

turns.speaker: Vinay Anupindi
turns.text: Monee is developing a way to settle large financial transactions using new technology. Our idea involved issuing investments and completing transactions in a way existing rules didn't clearly cover. We needed a serious regulator involved: this isn't a part of the financial system where you can just experiment and hope nothing goes wrong.

evidence.quote: Today, we are building wholesale sterling settlement infrastructure for tokenised markets.

Our innovation was at the edge of the regulatory perimeter. We were talking about issuing securities and settling it on innovative technology, which required actual regulatory guidance and perhaps even new laws made.
This was the sort of thing where you could not break things because this had to do with the actual capital market system, so we definitely saw a need for a regulator.

turns.speaker: Nick Tracey
turns.text: Bourn is developing an alternative to a business overdraft. We knew we'd need permission to process payments and possibly hold customers' e-money. We wanted to work with large UK banks, so applying for authorisation ourselves seemed more credible than operating through another authorised firm.

evidence.quote: We are developing an alternative to the business overdraft for SMEs that want to grow and we participated in the regulatory sandbox in 2025.
We knew that regulatory permissions would be required.

You can either pursue authorisation as a direct route, or seek to be an agent of an existing authorised entity. We wanted to partner with large UK-regulated banks, in order to go to market with our product proposition. We decided that direct authorisation was the more credible route

chapters.title: Does testing lead to permission?
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses had sharply different experiences of how clearly sandboxes set goals and connect testing to authorisation.

turns.speaker: Lord Sharkey
turns.text: The Startup Coalition says sandboxes lack published measures of success and, most importantly, don't connect properly to authorisation. Does that match your experience?

evidence.quote: It said some very positive things about sandboxes, but it made three criticisms. The first was that there is no published success framework and therefore no way to judge any of this, talking about sandboxes in general.
The chief criticism from the coalition’s written evidence is that the sandbox does not connect to authorisations and that is its central failure.

turns.speaker: Lyubomira Dimitrova
turns.text: We set our own goal: develop a product we could launch, working with firms that might use it. We haven't had a conversation with the sandbox team about what success would look like, or a check-in on our progress. We offered to demonstrate what we'd built, but they didn't take up the offer.

evidence.quote: In our application we were very explicit that we were looking to develop a commercial product that, by the end of the sandbox, we would want to launch and that, as part of our sandbox participation, we wanted to bring in design partners to work with from industry.
At no point did we discuss what success looks like with the current team running the sandbox we are in.
We offered to do a demo of what we are building and share insights. We were not taken up on the offer.

turns.speaker: Kevin Sefton
turns.text: Our goal was straightforward: get regulated. We did leave the sandbox successfully, although the process wasn't fully defined. But I'd also hoped to work with other firms in our group and make useful connections with financial institutions. That didn't really happen, and I don't know whether those institutions valued our sandbox experience.

evidence.quote: From our point of view, we wanted regulation. That was very clear. It provided that route and we exited the sandbox successfully. That was a fairly straightforward process, although a little bit undefined.
I thought that that might give us a cohort experience. We did not get a cohort experience.
Did they value the sandbox experience? I am not sure that they necessarily did.

turns.speaker: Vinay Anupindi
turns.text: Our experience differs. In the digital securities sandbox and the stablecoin sandbox, the published plans are detailed: the aim is to get licensed and start operating. Regulators are still developing the relevant rules, and we can contribute while they do. We aren't authorised yet, but we know what the intended exit is.

evidence.quote: In our particular case, with the digital securities sandbox and the stablecoin sandbox, I can say that there was a very detailed published framework. The objective of the sandboxes is to get licensed and go live in terms of issuing or settling securities.
the regulators and authorities are actively building policy, in which we got to participate within the sandbox.
Unlike my colleagues over here, we have not been authorised yet. We are still in the testing phase

turns.speaker: Nick Tracey
turns.text: The sandbox doesn't replace authorisation, but in our case the FCA teams handling testing and authorisation worked well together. We first got limited permission to test, then applied to remove those limits. We're now fully authorised to handle e-money. Each permission stage took about three months; including the testing period, the whole route took a year.

evidence.quote: I do not think that the sandbox is intended to be a replacement for authorisation, but we saw that the FCA innovation team that runs the sandbox was very well co-ordinated with the authorisations team

Initially we gained restricted permissions in order to undertake regulated activity while in the sandbox. On exiting the sandbox, we submitted a variation of permissions to remove those restrictions and therefore become a fully authorised EMI.

The total application was three months for the initial restricted permissions and an additional three months for the full or variation of permissions, so in total six months, or, end to end, including our regulatory sandbox testing, 12 months.

turns.speaker: Lord Hill of Oareford
turns.text: Did going through the sandbox actually speed up your authorisation, or might you just have been lucky?

evidence.quote: Do you think that the authorisation process is expedited as a result of being in the sandbox, if you see what I mean, so you have been through the sandbox, they know you and then your authorisation period gets a bit reduced, or were you just lucky?

turns.speaker: Nick Tracey
turns.text: I think there's a connection. During testing, we showed that the product worked, collected customer feedback and developed the safeguards we'd need for full authorisation. We met the FCA's innovation team monthly. I can't see exactly what passed between its teams, but the process felt well coordinated and timely.

evidence.quote: One was to technically test that the product worked and that customer feedback was positive. The other was to give us time to develop the controls and capabilities that we would need to demonstrate that we were ready to be fully authorised as an EMI.
We had a monthly meeting with FCA innovation where we were able to demonstrate customer feedback and technical viability, but also the control environment that we were building internally.
We did not see a lot of that, but our experience was that it was well joined up. The end-to-end one-year application process felt timely.

chapters.title: The work behind the test
chapters.takeaway: Applying could take considerable effort, and what firms could do once admitted varied from testing with artificial data to serving a limited number of real customers.

turns.speaker: Baroness Bowles of Berkhamsted
turns.text: How much work and money did it take to apply? Did you need outside help?

evidence.quote: When applying to the sandbox, was it resource intensive and did you find that you needed to get outside advisers to help you get your application through? Was that costly as well? There is resource in cash and resource in people.

turns.speaker: Nick Tracey
turns.text: It took our three founders about three months to prepare, with help from a part-time compliance specialist. We submitted more than 100 pages. That was demanding, but much of it was work we'd have needed to do anyway to become a regulated business.

evidence.quote: We spent around three months preparing an application to the regulatory sandbox. We were, at that stage, just a concept with three co-founders and no team. We hired a fractional compliance officer to support us with preparation of the application.

We submitted probably in excess of 100 pages, so not just the application form but also supporting documents. A lot of that would have been work that we would have needed to do anyway to be a regulated entity

turns.speaker: Vinay Anupindi
turns.text: Ours took a lot of time and attention too, which we think was appropriate. We were a small, self-funded team and couldn't afford professional help, so we read the requirements ourselves and asked regulators when we had questions.

evidence.quote: Yes, it was resource intensive, and we believe it should be. It was intensive in terms of time and actual focus given towards the application process.
We did not take any professional help. We could not afford that. We are bootstrapped still. Basically, we just went at it ourselves. If we had any questions, we asked the regulators.

turns.speaker: Kevin Sefton
turns.text: Our initial form took about five hours, but acceptance took five months. Then we discovered that admission wasn't permission to start testing: we still had to prepare a substantial business plan and obtain registration. That added roughly 80 to 100 hours of writing. It was valuable thinking, but it wasn't the quick entry we'd imagined.

evidence.quote: It was five hours’ effort to fill in a form initially, but we had already built most of the business. It then took five months, having filled that in, before we were actually approved.
although we were approved to be in the sandbox, we still needed to write all the documentation to get authorisation as well.
That took us probably 80 to 100 hours of effort, so two solid weeks writing that.
Then we got the registration confirmed and were in the sandbox.

turns.speaker: Lyubomira Dimitrova
turns.text: Our application was less demanding. Most of our effort went into deciding what problem to tackle and what to test. Someone who'd been through a sandbox gave us unpaid advice, and the programme lead gave us useful feedback before we applied.

evidence.quote: Compared to the effort these firms had to go through, ours was less. We spent most of the time thinking about the problem and scoping the project.
We used an adviser, not paid, just friendly, who helped us write the application. They were someone who participated in a sandbox.

We managed to get a meeting prior to our application with the lead of our current sandbox to run through, “This is what we are thinking. This is what we would like to test. Is that interesting? Is that viable?” They gave us feedback

turns.speaker: Lord Lilley
turns.text: Once you're inside, what can you actually do that you couldn't do outside?

evidence.quote: What are you allowed or not allowed to do that you would be allowed or not allowed to do if you were outside the sandbox?

turns.speaker: Lyubomira Dimitrova
turns.text: We can test our software against synthetic data—for example, made-up customer complaints—without using real customers' records. We also get computing support and mentors with experience in areas such as data protection and banking. That's valuable, though we'd have benefited from more time with someone expert in consumer duty itself.

evidence.quote: You have complaints data, so Ms Maria Dimitrova is writing a complaint about X, Y, Z. They have this dataset that we can use to test, for example, our technology.
As part of our sandbox, we also have credit with some of the cloud providers and some coding assistance.
The mentors are industry people.
One thing that we really wanted to do, and would have benefited from, is to have an expert in consumer duty working with us.

turns.speaker: Kevin Sefton
turns.text: Our sandbox was different. We had limited regulatory permission to offer our service to about 200 people. Once we could see it worked, the question became how to get full permission to serve more people. That's why it matters to say which kind of sandbox you're talking about.

evidence.quote: From our point of view, it was simply limited regulation that allowed us to support 200 people, and then we extended that to more. The key thing is what each sandbox is intended to achieve.
We realised quite quickly that it was working. Then how do we extend that to full regulation to allow us to be offering it to more people?

turns.speaker: Vinay Anupindi
turns.text: We supply our own simulated information for testing. In the stablecoin sandbox, we've met FCA staff every week or two to go through our technology, procedures and safeguards. Work in the digital securities sandbox has a longer timetable and less intensive meetings. The same word covers quite different arrangements.

evidence.quote: In fact, we had to give the regulators simulated data to show them testing in our case.

we had an intense cadence of every week or every two weeks where we would meet our case officer and the teams in the FCA, from policy and payments to financial crime, basically testing all our procedures
The other sandbox we are in is the digital securities sandbox, which is more focused with the Bank of England. It has not been as intense. It is more of a multi-year sandbox.

turns.speaker: Nick Tracey
turns.text: We could carry out regulated activities on a limited basis with real customers. Our six-month plan moved through launching the product, checking that it worked, gathering customer feedback and testing whether the system could cope as it grew. We discussed progress with the FCA roughly monthly.

evidence.quote: For the regulatory sandbox, we were able to undertake regulated activity on a limited basis to test our innovation.

Ours had around six phases, including launching technically the product, testing the technical effectiveness of the product, starting to test that with customers in live, recording customer feedback and stress testing for scalability and resilience of the platform that we built.
it was a six-month test for us, during which we had roughly monthly engagements with FCA innovation.

chapters.title: Who learns, and who benefits?
chapters.takeaway: Some witnesses saw two-way learning and stronger business prospects, while others were unsure whether their feedback reached regulators or brought lasting commercial benefits.

turns.speaker: Lord Eatwell
turns.text: Are regulators learning from you as well as helping you test your products? And does working with them reduce the risk that you'll invest in an idea only to be told later that the rules won't allow it?

evidence.quote: I am interested in not just what you got out of it, positive or negative, in the process, but also what the regulators got out of it.

You are making a lot of investment in developing new products and processes. There is a risk associated with this that the regulator will say, “Sorry, no”, and your money has just gone down a black hole.
Did you find in the process, or are you finding in the process in the case of Ms Dimitrova, that the regulators were learning and that this was a learning experience for them?

turns.speaker: Lyubomira Dimitrova
turns.text: I can't tell whether the regulator is learning from us. Our group of firms has met only twice, and we mostly work separately. We asked to be introduced to firms we thought we could work with, without success. We offered feedback too, but I haven't seen evidence that it's being used.

evidence.quote: In our cohort right now, we had two touchpoints or opportunities to gather as a cohort and meet each other. That was at the kick-off and at a mid-point meeting. Beyond that, it is a very siloed experience.
We asked to be introduced to a couple of other firms where we think we can work together to prove a point for both firms. We were not introduced.
Maybe they are taking learnings and feedback, both on what is working operationally and on the technological side, but, in full honesty, I do not have evidence of that.

turns.speaker: Kevin Sefton
turns.text: I hope the FCA has learned; its approach has changed since we participated, though I can't say that's because of us. Regulators need to learn about both the possibilities and the risks. But firms also need some benefit for investing time in that discussion. Otherwise, they might help establish that an idea is safe only for everyone else to enter the market at the same moment.

evidence.quote: I am hopeful that they have learned, because things have changed since we took part. It might well be that that is based on feedback from us. A regulator learning from a sandbox is an essential part of a sandbox.
a sandbox has a role with some trusted conversations between innovators and a regulator about what innovation may do, but also, quite frankly, around the risks of that innovation.
You do not want to find that the day that you are authorised to be conducting business is the day that everybody else is authorised as well.

turns.speaker: Vinay Anupindi
turns.text: In our case, both sides are learning. We've improved our procedures against regulators' expectations, and we've seen suggestions taken into account as rules develop. But we're still testing, not authorised, and I haven't seen evidence that participation will make our authorisation faster.

evidence.quote: I believe that we are both learning at the same time, definitely so in our case.
We found that we were able to make suggestions that they took note of. We have seen this being implemented as policy as well while we were working in the sandbox.
Unlike my colleagues over here, we have not been authorised yet. We are still in the testing phase, so we do not see any expedition in terms of us getting authorised.

turns.speaker: Nick Tracey
turns.text: The FCA team seemed genuinely curious about what we were doing. For instance, it introduced us to its open banking specialists so we could exchange ideas. From our side, it felt like a two-way conversation.

evidence.quote: it appeared to be collaborative, genuinely curious about the innovations that we were bringing forward and keen to learn from what we were doing.
it introduced us to the open banking specialists within the FCA to share ideas in a two-way setting.

turns.speaker: Lord Griffiths of Fforestfach
turns.text: Has being in a sandbox helped you raise money or attract the people and partners you need?

evidence.quote: As you reflect on having been in the sandbox, do you think that it has given you a competitive advantage in terms of raising money, attracting the right people, et cetera?

turns.speaker: Nick Tracey
turns.text: I believe it helped us. We became fully authorised, attracted attention from major banks and partnered with NatWest, which invested in us. We also raised £3.5 million around the time we left the sandbox. I think participation and the publicity helped give partners and investors confidence, although I can't separate out each factor.

evidence.quote: We attracted attention from tier 1 banks, I think partly due to our participation in the sandbox and associated publicity. We secured a strategic partnership with NatWest Group and it took a strategic investment in us as well.
We were able to close a £3.5 million seed investment round around the same time as us exiting the sandbox successfully.
giving investors and our bank partners the confidence that we were ready to scale that proposition.

turns.speaker: Vinay Anupindi
turns.text: It's yes and no for us. We haven't raised money. We can speak to regulators and test while the rules are being developed, which may give us some information sooner than firms waiting on the sidelines. But once the rules are established, better-funded competitors can apply too. I don't expect a lasting advantage.

evidence.quote: We have not been able to raise money yet, so I do not know whether that is an advantage there.

The only real advantage is that we get to test this and operate right now in a manner where we are discussing with the regulators. Maybe that gives us a little bit of an information advantage, but, in terms of execution or operation, I do not see that as a permanent advantage.
Once the regime goes live, I am sure that a horde of other firms that are much better resourced than we are will be doing the same applications to be authorised.

turns.speaker: Kevin Sefton
turns.text: I'm not sure the sandbox itself gave us a direct competitive advantage. Other firms could soon use an authorised company as an agent instead of getting FCA permission themselves, and I don't think investors or financial institutions fully appreciated what we'd done. We did receive support from a separate industry fund, probably partly because of our sandbox experience.

evidence.quote: The agent model that was discussed earlier is a much shorter-cut route to achieving exactly the same thing. In effect, you have one organisation that is fully regulated by the FCA and it allows others to act through its authorisation as agents.
I am not sure, as I said at the time, that any of the investors or financial institutions that we were talking to really appreciated what we were doing and going through.

We got supported through that probably as a result of our participation in the sandbox and the understanding of the rigours associated with that, so there is a knock-on effect. Did we get direct competitive advantage from being in the sandbox? With respect to the FCA, I have to say that I am not entirely sure.

turns.speaker: Lyubomira Dimitrova
turns.text: For us, the publicity and trust have helped persuade potential customers to consider a developing product. We've built it during our four months in the sandbox, using its data and mentors. It's too early for me to say whether that becomes a competitive advantage.

evidence.quote: the publicity helps, especially if you are an early-stage business. The trust helps to attract companies or customers that are willing to take a chance on a developing technology
We managed to build our product in the past four months while in the sandbox. We started with zero and built in the sandbox with the datasets, mentors and support.
On whether it provides a competitive advantage, it is too early for me to say and provide feedback.

chapters.title: What should change?
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses wanted each sandbox's purpose to be clearer, but differed on whether UK programmes already offer a credible route beyond testing.

turns.speaker: Lord Davies of Brixton
turns.text: You used the phrases “innovation theatre” and “mythic status” to describe some programmes and perceptions of sandboxes. What did you mean?

evidence.quote: One was “innovation theatre” from Mr Anupindi and the other was the “mythic status” of sandboxes from Mr Sefton.
I wondered whether you would like to expound a bit more on them.

turns.speaker: Vinay Anupindi
turns.text: After an unsuccessful FCA application in 2020, we explored other countries. Some welcomed firms but gave us no answer to full applications, or no clear route from joining a programme to becoming licensed. By contrast, the UK's digital securities sandbox appeared to come with plans for rules and a route to operating. That's why we chose to work here, though progress isn't as fast as everyone would like.

evidence.quote: We applied in 2020 and did not get in, which, by the way, was quite early and even pre Covid.
Examples would be that we would give full applications and not even get answers as to whether we got in.
Then there was not much towards where this is going: “How will we get authorised? How will this scale? What are the plans of the authorities to make this into a sustained industry?”
We saw that there was actual intent and seriousness, not just in having a sandbox but actual pathways to being licensed. There were policies and laws being made.
things are progressing, maybe not at the pace that many in the industry might like

turns.speaker: Kevin Sefton
turns.text: I borrowed “mythic status” from an earlier witness. People talk about the benefits of the FCA sandbox without always asking what it actually does. I've also seen large financial firms celebrate innovation and invite small businesses to present, only for it to be hard to find anyone who'll work with them afterwards. A programme needs a clear purpose and practical follow-through.

evidence.quote: I do not want to take credit for that line. I think it came from one of your previous witnesses.
We will find ourselves paraded and presenting to them in a big room, but, when it comes to follow-up, trying to find the right person in a large organisation is a challenge.
I hear lots of people referring to the benefits of the FCA sandbox without truly understanding what it is or even inquiring about what it is.
needs to understand what the purpose is and therefore what the right combination of interventions is to achieve those goals.

turns.speaker: Nick Tracey
turns.text: Our experience with big banks was different. We partnered with Investec and then NatWest while in the sandbox. I wonder whether its supervised setting made it easier for them to work with a firm as young as ours.

evidence.quote: We were able to partner with two banks—Investec and then NatWest Group—during our time in the sandbox. I wonder whether it would have been possible for them to take that chance on such an early-stage firm if it had not been for that framework.

turns.speaker: Lord Davies of Brixton
turns.text: If being admitted can help a firm, how does the FCA decide who gets in? Do you know whether it treats applicants fairly?

evidence.quote: the acceptance into the sandbox is quite an important element. I am curious to understand how you see the FCA choosing which people to take into the sandbox. Do you think it is even-handed? Is it trying to pick winners, or how is it doing it?

turns.speaker: Lyubomira Dimitrova
turns.text: I don't know why our proposal was selected. We didn't receive feedback explaining that decision.

evidence.quote: We did not hear feedback necessarily about why we were chosen, so I really do not know.

turns.speaker: Nick Tracey
turns.text: We saw the FCA's published criteria and wrote our application around them, but we didn't get feedback about its particular strengths or weaknesses.

evidence.quote: We did not receive any feedback on specifically what the strengths or weaknesses of our application were. We saw the criteria published on the FCA’s website and aimed to answer those points when we applied.

turns.speaker: Lord Hill of Oareford
turns.text: Do you know of a case where a sandbox participant's experience led the FCA to change an underlying rule, rather than simply helping the firm meet it?

evidence.quote: do any of you—you do not all have to answer—have any examples of where, as a result of a company or business being in a sandbox and going through the sandbox, the FCA changed any underlying regulation?
All it is, otherwise, is a way of helping you to accommodate what it is that they require you to do, which may or may not be sensible.

turns.speaker: Vinay Anupindi
turns.text: I can't name a particular firm that caused a change. Rules in our area are still being developed, and we've seen changes that some firms welcome and others don't. I think regulators are listening to industry, while also weighing their responsibility to protect the financial system and its users.

evidence.quote: I cannot think of a specific firm, but right now the policies and legislation for our particular innovation industry are quite fluid. We have seen things that have already changed. Some firms in our industry are glad to see those changes. Some other firms are not glad
we feel that the regulators are taking a very sensible approach to this and listening to industry. There is a balance on how much they can take into account what industry suggests.
they need to maintain stability and prudential care, and make sure Nan is not hurt financially.

turns.speaker: Baroness Donaghy
turns.text: Is the word “sandbox” itself obscuring the differences? Would it help new firms more if we explained the different kinds clearly—or even stopped using the word?

evidence.quote: We could write a report that clearly defines all those different possibilities of a sandbox, or we could write one sentence that says, “We think the financial world should ban the word ‘sandbox’”. What do you think would be the most helpful to the financial world and to your companies, just setting off for the first time?

turns.speaker: Lyubomira Dimitrova
turns.text: Defining each programme's purpose would help. We're building technology, not seeking authorisation, so we need different support from firms applying for permission. I'd like more chances for participating firms to meet, more opportunity to give feedback, and access to a regulator with expertise in the rule we're trying to help firms follow. The sandbox is useful; it could be much better.

evidence.quote: We are a technology provider. We are not a firm seeking to be authorised, so our profile is very different and we would benefit from a different type of support
we are missing an opportunity here even just to have more informal check-ins and gatherings to exchange ideas and feedback
if you are interested in a topic such as consumer duty technology, have an expert on consumer duty who is interested in enabling the market
It is a useful tool. It works. It can work better.

turns.speaker: Kevin Sefton
turns.text: The confusion matters. In technology, a sandbox can simply mean a place to try out a system; ours was a route to limited regulatory permission. If everyone means something different, they may choose the wrong tool for the job. I don't know the best replacement word, but the committee shouldn't overlook the problem.

evidence.quote: The word “sandbox” is so confusing. Please do not ignore that confusion in the report.
The word “sandbox” in technology terms means basically a place that you can connect your systems to and play around with. Just the one word is really unhelpful.
From our point of view, it was simply limited regulation that allowed us to support 200 people

turns.speaker: Vinay Anupindi
turns.text: “Sandbox” has become a catch-all name for programmes with different aims. In our case, it really is a way to test something new: there wasn't an existing permission we could simply apply for. But joining hasn't given us special treatment in authorisation; that decision remains with the authorisation team.

evidence.quote: “Sandbox” has become a catch-all word to describe many different things. In essence, they are innovation programmes and I suppose each programme has its own objectives and requirements.
There was not a way for us to just ignore the sandbox and go for direct authorisation, because direct authorisation does not exist.
Whether it helps is up to the authorisation team.

turns.speaker: Lord Smith of Kelvin
turns.text: Beyond those examples, did anyone find a useful approach in another country?

evidence.quote: Does anyone have anything to share about other jurisdictions?

turns.speaker: Vinay Anupindi
turns.text: Our overseas experiences weren't all negative: Ireland's central-bank sandbox was useful. But in some places we couldn't see what would happen after admission, and we felt larger established firms were preferred. In the UK, we've been able to participate alongside those firms without encountering that kind of barrier.

turns.text: We also spoke to regulators in Belgium because we weren't sure how long our FCA application would take. We could quickly arrange a meeting and talk through the process, which was encouraging, though we didn't go on to apply there.

evidence.quote: We looked at Belgium, because we were unsure about the timing of the FCA application process and did not want all our eggs in one basket.
